title: Duck typing and shape-based APIs
hook: JavaScript never asks what class an object is — it asks whether the object can do the job. If your value has the right properties and methods at the moment you call them, the engine proceeds; if not, you get a runtime TypeError.

blocks.text: **Duck typing** means compatibility is decided by **shape and behavior**, not by a declared type name. An object is usable if it exposes the members your code touches — `length`, `push`, `then`, or a custom `validate()` method. JavaScript has no compile-time interface check; the engine walks the **prototype chain** at property access time. TypeScript adds **structural typing** at compile time, but that erases — at runtime you still have duck typing only.

entries.plainDefinition: If it behaves like the expected shape, treat it as compatible — no explicit implements clause.
entries.example: function logLength(x) { console.log(x.length); } // works on string, array, { length: 3 }

entries.plainDefinition: TypeScript checks that required properties exist on a value's shape, not that it extends a named class.
entries.example: type HasId = { id: string }; function save(x: HasId) { ... }

entries.plainDefinition: Any object with a callable then method — await treats it like a Promise.
Object with numeric keys and length — duck-types as array for some APIs but lacks Array.prototype methods.
entries.example: function fn() { console.log(arguments.length); } // arguments is array-like

blocks.text: Libraries accept **minimal shapes** on purpose: fetch accepts Request-like objects, React components accept props objects, and Node streams accept anything with `write`/`end`. Misunderstanding duck typing causes production bugs — passing a plain object where an array method is expected, or assuming `instanceof Array` covers cross-realm arrays from iframes. C# developers expect **nominal** types; in JS you validate at boundaries or pay with undefined and TypeError at 2 a.m.

blocks.title: Interview trap: instanceof versus shape
blocks.body: instanceof fails across realms and ignores interface-like objects. Senior answer: prefer shape checks (Array.isArray, typeof x.then === 'function') or schema validation at API edges.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Call site expects a shape
items.body: Your function reads obj.id or calls obj.map — no upfront type proof.

items.title: Engine resolves property
items.body: Own properties first, then prototype chain until found or undefined.

items.title: Callable check
items.body: If you invoke the value, it must be typeof 'function' or TypeError.

items.title: Failure is late
items.body: Missing members surface when accessed, not when the object was created.

diagram.title: Duck typing at a call site
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[Value passed in] --> B{Has required property?}
  B -->|yes| C[Use value]
  B -->|no| D[undefined or TypeError]
  C --> E{Method callable?}
  E -->|no| F[TypeError at invoke]
  E -->|yes| G[Success]

snippet.label: Same function, many shapes
snippet.explanation: printLength never checks a type name — only that .length resolves. Empty object returns undefined, not an error.

snippet.label: Thenable duck typing with await
snippet.explanation: await accepts any thenable, not only Promise instances — critical when integrating older callback libraries.

snippet.label: C# nominal typing contrast
snippet.explanation: C# requires explicit interface implementation at compile time. JS accepts any object with a length property at runtime.

snippet.label: Failure mode: array-like without .map
snippet.explanation: Duck typing is partial — length alone does not make an Array. Array.isArray or explicit conversion is the safe guard.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using instanceof Array on values from another window or Worker. Assuming JSON.parse output matches your interface without validation. Over-trusting optional chaining when the missing property means a logic bug, not a benign undefined.

blocks.text: Production proof: log shape failures at service boundaries with structured errors (400 + field path), not generic 500s. In design review, document **required shapes** as TypeScript types plus runtime schema (Zod/io-ts) because TS cannot protect JSON.parse. Know that V8 uses **hidden classes** — objects with stable shape are faster; duck typing still works but chaotic key order hurts IC (inline cache) hits.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'JavaScript is untyped so anything goes' without mentioning structural checks, thenables, or boundary validation. Cannot explain why instanceof fails for cross-realm arrays. Claiming TypeScript replaces runtime validation for external input.

interviewTakeaways: Duck typing: compatibility by shape and behavior at runtime, not by declared class name.
await accepts thenables — not only Promise instances — which matters for legacy interop.
Production: validate external JSON; use Array.isArray and typeof guards on hot paths.
60s: JS checks shape when you access properties. TS adds compile-time structural typing that erases. C# is nominal. Validate at API boundaries; instanceof Array fails cross-realm.
Follow-up: how would you type and validate a webhook payload in Node without trusting the client?
commonPitfalls: Using instanceof for arrays or custom types without mentioning cross-realm and shape edge cases.
Treating TypeScript interfaces as runtime guarantees for fetch/JSON data.
Strong answer: duck typing at runtime, structural TS at compile, schema validation at boundaries, Array.isArray over instanceof.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript interface compatibility is structural — if it has the members, it fits. That mirrors JS runtime duck typing but only before emit.
Promise.resolve and await duck-type on .then — same pattern as accepting minimal stream or iterable shapes in library APIs.
